broader_review_uses.connection_to_review: Contextual background on the evolution of microbiome-immunotherapy research
broader_review_uses.material: Historical perspective section tracing discoveries from 2007 to 2025, highlighting the shift from correlation to mechanistic understanding and clinical trials.
broader_review_uses.purpose: To provide a timeline of key advancements and justify the current interest in microbiome modulation as a critical factor in immunotherapy success.

broader_review_uses.connection_to_review: Discussion of intervention strategies beyond just biomarkers
broader_review_uses.material: Sections on FMT, probiotics, antibiotics, diet, and engineered microbes, including tables of clinical trials.
broader_review_uses.purpose: To illustrate potential therapeutic avenues for overcoming ICI resistance and managing toxicity, providing examples of how microbiome modulation is being translated into clinical practice.

broader_review_uses.connection_to_review: Challenges and limitations in the field
broader_review_uses.material: Section on 'Challenges and future directions' discussing technical variability, donor effects in FMT, host genetics, and lack of standardization.
broader_review_uses.purpose: To highlight methodological hurdles and confounding factors that must be considered when interpreting microbiome-ICI associations, explaining why consistent biomarkers are hard to identify.

facet_contributions.boundaries: Associations are largely correlative from retrospective or small prospective cohorts. Specificity varies by cancer type and ICI agent. Lack of standardized detection methods limits direct comparison. Does not establish causality.
facet_contributions.contribution: Identifies specific gut microbial taxa associated with ICI response or resistance in solid tumors. For example, Akkermansia muciniphila, Bifidobacterium, and Ruminococcaceae are linked to better outcomes in melanoma and NSCLC, while certain Proteobacteria or high abundance of Bacteroides intestinalis may correlate with resistance or toxicity. It also notes that beneficial taxa vary by ICI type (anti-PD-1 vs. anti-CTLA-4) and cancer type.
facet_contributions.possible_uses: Can be used to list candidate microbial biomarkers for predicting ICI efficacy in solid tumors. Helps explain inter-patient variability in treatment response.

facet_contributions.boundaries: Many mechanisms are primarily demonstrated in mouse models (preclinical). Human validation is often indirect or observational. Some mechanisms (e.g., molecular mimicry) are proposed but require further confirmation in humans. Effects can be bidirectional (promoting or suppressing immunity depending on context).
facet_contributions.contribution: Details mechanisms by which gut microbiota modulate ICI efficacy: 1) Direct immune modulation via PRR activation (TLR/NLR) leading to DC maturation and T-cell activation; 2) Metabolite-mediated regulation (SCFAs inhibiting HDAC, bile acids affecting Th17/Treg balance, tryptophan metabolites via AhR); 3) Molecular mimicry where bacterial antigens cross-react with tumor antigens; 4) Remodeling of the tumor microenvironment (TME) through intratumoral bacteria or systemic metabolites influencing tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS).
facet_contributions.possible_uses: Provides mechanistic explanations for how the microbiome influences ICI response. Supports the biological rationale for microbiome-targeted interventions.

planning_summary: This review serves as a foundational resource for mapping the relationship between gut microbiome composition and ICI efficacy in solid tumors. It provides specific microbial markers (taxa) associated with response/resistance, details mechanistic pathways (metabolites, immune cell crosstalk), and outlines current intervention strategies (FMT, probiotics, diet). It is particularly useful for identifying candidate biomarkers and understanding the biological plausibility of microbiome-mediated modulation, while also highlighting the methodological challenges and variability that complicate definitive conclusions.
scope_interpretation_cautions: The review covers both gut and intratumoral microbiota; ensure distinction is maintained when applying findings to 'gut microbiome' specific facets.

Findings on specific bacterial taxa are highly dependent on the cancer type (e.g., melanoma vs. NSCLC) and the specific ICI agent (anti-PD-1 vs. anti-CTLA-4); avoid over-generalizing across all solid tumors.
Many mechanistic insights are derived from murine models; caution is needed when extrapolating to human physiology without explicit human validation mentioned in the text.
Clinical trial data cited are often from early-phase (I/II) or small cohorts; results should not be interpreted as definitive proof of efficacy for interventions like FMT or probiotics.
title: Gut microbiota shapes cancer immunotherapy responses
